title: Philoptics Wins New Global Order for 2.0mm Glass Substrate TGV Equipment With Zero Defects
content:
Korea Supply Chain Brief · September 29, 2026

Philoptics (KOSDAQ: 161580) won an order for next-generation TGV equipment from a new global customer, after its machine processed 2.0mm-thick glass substrates — a harder, thicker format than today's standard — with a zero-defect rate in customer testing. Here is what TGV is, why the thicker glass matters, and what was and was not disclosed.

CompanyRoleEvidence
Philoptics
KOSDAQ: 161580		Maker of TGV processing and AOI inspection equipment for glass substratesAnnounced (company release, Sep 29, 2026)

What was announced

  • Order won: next-generation TGV (Through Glass Via) equipment, sized for 2.0mm-thick glass substrate panels.
  • Qualification result: in evaluation on full production-size 510mm x 515mm glass panels, the equipment achieved 0 ppm defects while meeting the customer's targets for aspect ratio and waist-to-top diameter ratio — two of the hardest metrics in via drilling.
  • Bundled sale: the customer is also buying Philoptics' AOI (automated optical inspection) equipment, to inspect for defects immediately after the TGV drilling step.
  • Customer identity: not disclosed. Philoptics calls it a "new global customer" and a company that "leads the global supply chain," but names no company. We do not name a customer here because none was disclosed.

What TGV is and why 2.0mm glass is the harder version

TGV (Through Glass Via) is the process of drilling thousands of microscopic holes through a glass substrate so electrical connections can pass through it — the glass-substrate equivalent of via drilling in a conventional circuit board, and a prerequisite for using glass as a chip packaging material at all. Glass substrates are being developed as a successor to today's plastic (organic) substrates because glass is flatter and more dimensionally stable, which matters more as AI chips get larger and packages get denser.

Thicker glass (2.0mm here, versus thinner standard panels) resists warping better, which is useful for large AI packages. But it makes the TGV process harder: drilling a deeper, higher-aspect-ratio hole while keeping its shape consistent from top to bottom (the "waist" measurement) is more failure-prone, and the following step — filling the hole with copper — carries a higher risk of voids (gaps) as the hole gets deeper. Philoptics said in the release that as glass gets thicker, warpage control improves but the difficulty of hole shaping and copper-filling rises sharply, and called reliable TGV quality "the fundamental starting point" for raising yield across the whole glass substrate supply chain.

Why this order matters beyond one machine sale

Philoptics frames the order as evidence that adoption is moving faster than expected: it says U.S. and Taiwanese semiconductor companies that had been watching the glass substrate market from the sidelines are now moving toward adopting it for next-generation packaging, which could pull forward the commercialization timeline. The company has supplied mass-production glass substrate equipment since 2022 and says it is now expanding beyond substrate makers to other companies across the glass substrate value chain.

What is not disclosed

  • The customer's name, nationality, or which chip or product line the equipment will serve.
  • The dollar or won value of the order.
  • A delivery or mass-production timeline for this specific order.

Quick FAQ

What did Philoptics just win?
An order for next-generation TGV (via-drilling) equipment for 2.0mm-thick glass substrates, plus AOI inspection equipment, from an unnamed new global customer.

What is TGV?
Through Glass Via: the process of drilling and copper-filling tiny holes through a glass substrate so it can carry electrical signals, required for glass to be used as an AI chip packaging material.

Why is 2.0mm glass significant?
It resists warping better than thinner glass, which helps with large AI chip packages, but makes precise via drilling and copper-filling substantially harder — Philoptics says it hit 0 ppm defects on this thicker format in customer testing.

Is this the same customer as prior glass substrate news?
Not stated. Philoptics did not name the customer in this release.
